Unit 1 The Global Tapestry

Unit 1 Context CardThe World in c. 1200By c. 1200, regional states across Afro-Eurasia used belief systems, taxation, trade, and specialized administration to organize diverse populations.Exam SkillsContextualizationComparison

As you study Unit 1, compare the material foundations of state power with the cultural ideas rulers used to legitimize authority.

  • Song China connected centralized administration to commercial growth and infrastructure.
  • States in Dar al-Islam, South Asia, and Southeast Asia adapted shared religious traditions to local political needs.
  • West African rulers converted control of trade into revenue, military capacity, and prestige.

Song Commercial Revolution

960–1279

Region

Hangzhou · Asia

Summary

Song rule encouraged production for markets, expanded cities, and connected regional exchange to Hangzhou.

Why It Matters

Commercialization made urban demand, specialized production, and long-distance exchange central features of Song prosperity and state revenue.

Use It on the Exam

Use this case to explain how state stability and expanding markets changed economic life in East Asia during the period c. 1200–1450.

Key Terms (2)
commercialization
The growing production of goods for sale through markets rather than only for local subsistence.
tribute system
A diplomatic framework that also supported regulated exchange between China and neighboring states.
Evidence (2)
  • Song China supported a large urban population whose demand encouraged specialized craft and agricultural production.
  • Hangzhou became a major political and commercial center linked to both inland and maritime exchange.
Connections (2)

Cause

Effect

People (1)
Emperor Taizu
Founded the Song dynasty and established the political order in which commercial expansion developed.
Source (1)

Grand Canal and the Hangzhou Market

1000–1279

Region

Hangzhou · Asia

Summary

The Grand Canal carried grain and goods toward Hangzhou and helped sustain a large southern urban market.

Why It Matters

Canal transport joined productive regions to consumers and officials, allowing the Song state to provision cities and collect resources across its territory.

Use It on the Exam

Use the Grand Canal as evidence that government infrastructure could integrate regional economies and support urban growth in Song China.

Key Terms (2)
Grand Canal
The inland waterway that linked northern and southern Chinese economic regions.
urbanization
The growth of cities as centers of administration, consumption, production, and exchange.
Evidence (2)
  • Hangzhou stood near the southern end of the Grand Canal and received goods from a broad internal market.
  • Reliable water transport moved bulky grain more efficiently than overland shipment and supported large cities.
Connections (1)

Effect

People (1)
Song transport officials
Managed canal shipments and the movement of tax grain toward administrative and urban centers.
Source (1)

Paper Money and Maritime Technology

1100–1279

Region

Hangzhou · Asia

Summary

Paper money and improved navigation reduced transaction costs and helped Hangzhou connect with maritime Asia.

Why It Matters

Financial and navigational tools made trade easier to finance and safer to conduct, extending Song commercial influence beyond its internal market.

Use It on the Exam

Use these innovations to explain how financial practices and navigation technologies increased the scale of exchange in and beyond East Asia.

Key Terms (2)
paper money
Government-backed currency that reduced reliance on heavy strings of copper coins.
magnetic compass
A navigational instrument that helped mariners maintain direction beyond sight of land.
Evidence (2)
  • Song China expanded the use of paper currency in a highly monetized commercial economy.
  • Chinese mariners used the compass and improved ship design to navigate regional sea routes.
Connections (1)

Cause

People (1)
Song merchants
Used paper currency, credit practices, and maritime knowledge to conduct exchange over longer distances.
Source (1)

Baghdad as an Abbasid Knowledge Hub

750–1258

Region

Baghdad · Middle East and Central Asia

Summary

Abbasid Baghdad connected scholars who preserved and developed Greek, Persian, and Indian learning.

Why It Matters

Translation, scholarship, and urban patronage made Baghdad a major center for knowledge that circulated across the Islamic world and beyond.

Use It on the Exam

Use Baghdad to explain how states and cities preserved, combined, and transmitted knowledge across regional and religious boundaries.

Key Terms (2)
House of Wisdom
The name associated with Abbasid scholarly and translation activity in Baghdad.
ulama
Learned Muslim scholars who interpreted and taught Islamic religious and legal traditions.
Evidence (2)
  • Baghdad scholars translated and studied works drawn from Greek, Persian, and Indian traditions.
  • Abbasid patronage supported advances in mathematics, medicine, astronomy, and philosophy.
Connections (1)

Related Event

People (1)
al-Khwarizmi
A Baghdad-based scholar whose mathematical work helped develop algebra and transmit numerical methods.
Source (1)

Merchants, Ulama, and Islamic Trade

1000–1450

Region

Baghdad · Middle East and Central Asia

Summary

Merchants and religious scholars linked commercial practice, law, and trust across the Islamic world.

Why It Matters

Shared legal ideas and respect for commerce helped strangers transact across long distances despite political fragmentation after Abbasid decline.

Use It on the Exam

Use this network to explain how a shared religious and legal culture maintained continuity across politically divided Islamic states.

Key Terms (2)
sharia
Islamic moral and legal traditions that included rules relevant to contracts, property, and exchange.
diaspora
A community living away from its place of origin while maintaining social and commercial connections.
Evidence (2)
  • Merchants held respected positions in many Muslim societies and supported mosques, schools, and charitable institutions.
  • Ulama provided teaching and legal interpretation across states whose rulers and dynasties changed over time.
Connections (3)

Related Event

People (1)
Muslim merchants
Carried goods, commercial practices, and religious traditions through interconnected cities and ports.
Source (1)

Bhakti and Sufi Devotional Traditions

1100–1450

Region

Delhi · Asia

Summary

Bhakti teachers and Sufi mystics emphasized personal devotion and reached communities beyond formal religious elites.

Why It Matters

Devotional movements created shared practices and cultural exchange without eliminating the distinct institutions of Hinduism and Islam.

Use It on the Exam

Use Bhakti and Sufism to explain cultural interaction in South Asia while avoiding the claim that the two religions simply merged.

Key Terms (2)
Bhakti
A Hindu devotional tradition emphasizing a direct and loving relationship with a chosen deity.
Sufism
Mystical Islamic practices that emphasized personal experience, discipline, and closeness to God.
Evidence (2)
  • Bhakti devotion could bypass some ritual and social barriers by stressing an individual's relationship with a deity.
  • Sufi teachers formed communities that helped Islam take root through teaching and personal example.
Connections (2)

Related Event

People (1)
Nizamuddin Auliya
A prominent Chishti Sufi teacher in Delhi whose community emphasized devotion, service, and spiritual instruction.
Source (1)

Delhi Sultanate State Building

1206–1450

Region

Delhi · Asia

Summary

Turkic Muslim rulers governed from Delhi while ruling a large population that remained mainly Hindu.

Why It Matters

The sultanate created a durable Islamic state in northern India while relying on accommodation, military power, and existing local institutions.

Use It on the Exam

Use Delhi to explain how a religious minority could build a state by combining conquest with selective accommodation of local society.

Key Terms (2)
Delhi Sultanate
A sequence of Muslim-ruled dynasties governing much of northern India from Delhi.
jizya
A tax historically imposed by some Muslim governments on non-Muslim subjects.
Evidence (2)
  • A Muslim political minority governed territories whose population remained predominantly Hindu.
  • The sultanate preserved many local social practices even as it introduced Persianate and Islamic political traditions.
Connections (2)

Related Event

People (1)
Raziyya
Ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240 and demonstrated both the reach and limits of female sovereignty.
Source (1)

Angkor's Hydraulic State

802–1431

Region

Angkor · Asia

Summary

Khmer rulers organized reservoirs, canals, and labor around Angkor to manage water and support intensive rice agriculture.

Why It Matters

Control of water and labor produced agricultural surpluses that sustained Angkor, financed monumental building, and strengthened royal authority.

Use It on the Exam

Use Angkor to explain how rulers in South and Southeast Asia connected environmental management, agricultural surplus, and state building.

Key Terms (2)
baray
A large Khmer reservoir used within Angkorian systems of water storage and management.
hydraulic state
A state whose authority and resources are closely connected to organizing large water-control works.
Evidence (2)
  • Angkor contained extensive reservoirs and canals associated with managing seasonal water supplies.
  • Rice surpluses supported a dense capital and the labor required for temples and public works.
Connections (1)

Effect

People (1)
Jayavarman II
Established the Khmer imperial tradition that later rulers expanded around Angkor.
Source (1)

Hindu and Buddhist Legitimation at Angkor

1113–1431

Region

Angkor · Asia

Summary

Khmer rulers used Hindu and later Buddhist institutions and monuments to present kingship as sacred and protective.

Why It Matters

Religious adaptation let successive rulers claim continuity while changing traditions, tying political loyalty to temples, ritual, and royal patronage.

Use It on the Exam

Use this transition to explain how Southeast Asian states adapted imported religions to legitimize rulers and maintain political continuity.

Key Terms (2)
Angkor Wat
A monumental temple complex first dedicated to Vishnu and associated with Khmer royal power.
Theravada Buddhism
A Buddhist tradition that became increasingly influential in mainland Southeast Asia.
Evidence (2)
  • Angkor Wat joined religious symbolism, royal patronage, and monumental labor in one political landscape.
  • Khmer religious life shifted from strongly Hindu court traditions toward Buddhism without erasing Angkor as a sacred center.
Connections (1)

Cause

People (1)
Suryavarman II
Sponsored Angkor Wat and used monumental Hindu architecture to express royal authority.
Source (1)

Manorial Agriculture and Feudal Order

1200–1450

Region

Medieval Europe · London · Europe

Summary

London serves as a regional anchor for a Europe in which manors organized rural production and feudal ties distributed political and military obligations.

Why It Matters

These overlapping local institutions shaped political fragmentation and agricultural life even as monarchies, towns, and commerce gradually expanded.

Use It on the Exam

Use manorial and feudal relationships to contextualize Europe’s decentralized order and trace continuity alongside the later growth of towns and monarchies.

Key Terms (2)
manorialism
A rural economic and social system organized around an estate, its lord, and dependent peasant labor.
feudalism
A broad label for decentralized political relationships based on landholding, loyalty, and military obligation.
Evidence (2)
  • Most Europeans lived in agricultural communities where peasants owed rents or labor to landholding elites.
  • Kings often depended on nobles whose local land, castles, and armed followers limited centralized authority.
Connections (1)

Effect

People (1)
manorial lords and peasants
Negotiated rents, labor services, protection, and access to land within local agricultural communities.
Source (1)

Towns, Guilds, and Commercial Growth

1200–1450

Region

Medieval Europe · London · Europe

Summary

London serves as a representative map anchor for the broader European growth of towns and merchant and craft guilds that regulated economic life.

Why It Matters

Urban and commercial growth created institutions and social groups with interests extending beyond manorial agriculture and local noble authority.

Use It on the Exam

Use guilds and towns to explain how expanding commerce changed European social organization while many rural manorial practices continued.

Key Terms (2)
guild
An association of merchants or craftspeople that regulated standards, training, prices, and market access.
commercial growth
The expansion of markets, specialized production, money exchange, and long-distance trade.
Evidence (2)
  • Merchant guilds protected trade privileges, while craft guilds supervised apprenticeship and product standards.
  • London connected regional agricultural production with wider North Sea and European commercial networks.
Connections (1)

Cause

People (1)
guild members
Merchants and artisans who regulated occupations, trained apprentices, and defended collective privileges.
Source (1)

Magna Carta and Negotiated Monarchy

1215

Region

Medieval Europe · London · Europe

Summary

London and England serve as a representative map anchor for a European case of negotiated monarchy: English barons compelled King John to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede during political conflict.

Why It Matters

The charter expressed medieval elite bargaining and the principle that a monarch faced established legal constraints, not a system of modern democracy.

Use It on the Exam

Use Magna Carta to compare constraints on rulers while avoiding anachronism: it limited some royal behavior but did not create modern democracy.

Key Terms (2)
Magna Carta
A 1215 charter protecting specific baronial and ecclesiastical privileges and limiting some royal actions.
negotiated monarchy
Rule shaped by bargaining between a monarch and powerful groups whose cooperation the ruler needed.
Evidence (2)
  • The charter arose from a baronial revolt and chiefly protected the interests of nobles, the church, and other privileged groups.
  • Clauses required the king to observe inherited customs and forms of lawful judgment in specified disputes.
Connections (1)

Related Event

People (1)
King John
Accepted Magna Carta after conflict with English barons over failed wars, taxation, and arbitrary royal actions.
Source (1)

Chinampas and Urban State Capacity

1325–1450

Region

Aztec Empire · Tenochtitlan · Americas

Summary

Mexica farmers expanded chinampa agriculture around Tenochtitlan to support a dense island capital and its growing political power.

Why It Matters

Intensive lake agriculture generated reliable food surpluses that sustained urban specialists, armies, rulers, and the institutions of an expanding state.

Use It on the Exam

Use chinampas to explain how societies adapted environments and converted agricultural productivity into urban growth and state capacity.

Key Terms (2)
chinampa
A raised, highly productive agricultural plot constructed in the shallow waters of the Valley of Mexico.
Tenochtitlan
The Mexica island capital that became the center of the Aztec Empire.
Evidence (2)
  • Chinampas used fertile lake mud and carefully managed waterways to produce repeated harvests close to Tenochtitlan.
  • Agricultural surplus helped feed a large urban population that included artisans, merchants, priests, soldiers, and officials.
Connections (2)

Effect

Related Event

People (1)
Mexica farmers
Built and maintained raised agricultural plots that supplied maize, vegetables, and flowers to the capital.
Source (1)

Religion, Warfare, and Mexica Legitimacy

1325–1450

Region

Aztec Empire · Tenochtitlan · Americas

Summary

Mexica rulers linked warfare, tribute, and public religious ritual to a sacred story of their capital and empire.

Why It Matters

Religious ceremonies presented conquest and sacrifice as obligations within a cosmic order, helping rulers justify expansion and mobilize society.

Use It on the Exam

Use Mexica ritual and warfare to compare how rulers in different regions used belief systems and public display to legitimate political authority.

Key Terms (2)
Huitzilopochtli
The Mexica patron deity associated with the sun, warfare, and the sacred identity of Tenochtitlan.
human sacrifice
A state ritual that Mexica leaders connected to sustaining cosmic order and displaying political power.
Evidence (2)
  • The Templo Mayor placed state ceremony at the physical and symbolic center of Tenochtitlan.
  • Military campaigns supplied captives for ritual and demonstrated the ruler’s ability to defend and expand the sacred community.
Connections (1)

Cause

People (1)
Mexica priests
Conducted state rituals that connected military success and royal authority to the gods.
Source (1)

Triple Alliance and Tribute Empire

1428–1450

Region

Aztec Empire · Tenochtitlan · Americas

Summary

Tenochtitlan joined Texcoco and Tlacopan in the Triple Alliance and used conquest to collect tribute from subject communities.

Why It Matters

Tribute moved food, textiles, labor, and luxury goods toward the imperial center, strengthening rulers while creating resentment among subject peoples.

Use It on the Exam

Use the Triple Alliance to compare tribute-based imperial rule with other systems that extracted taxes, goods, or labor from subject populations.

Key Terms (2)
Triple Alliance
The political and military alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan formed in 1428.
tribute empire
An empire that leaves many conquered communities locally governed while requiring regular payments and obedience.
Evidence (2)
  • Conquered communities delivered specified goods such as maize, cloth, cacao, feathers, and military equipment.
  • The alliance concentrated an increasing share of tribute and influence in Tenochtitlan.
Connections (3)

Cause

Effect

Related Event

People (1)
Itzcoatl
Led Tenochtitlan during the formation of the Triple Alliance and the early expansion of its tribute power.
Source (1)

Ayllu, Mit'a, and State Labor

1438–1450

Region

Inca Empire · Cusco · Americas

Summary

Inca rulers organized ayllu communities through rotating mit'a labor obligations rather than relying on a money tax.

Why It Matters

The mit'a converted community labor into roads, terraces, armies, storehouses, and public works that expanded imperial capacity across the Andes.

Use It on the Exam

Use ayllu and mit'a to explain how the Inca mobilized labor and compare their system with tribute or tax collection in other empires.

Key Terms (2)
ayllu
An Andean kin-based community that shared land, obligations, and mutual support.
mit'a
A rotating labor obligation through which communities supplied workers to the Inca state.
Evidence (2)
  • Households supplied labor for farming state lands, military service, construction, and transport.
  • The state redistributed stored goods during campaigns, ceremonies, and periods of local need.
Connections (4)

Cause

Effect

Related Event

People (1)
ayllu leaders
Coordinated kin-based communities and helped allocate households for rotating state labor obligations.

Pachacuti and Tawantinsuyu

1438–1450

Region

Inca Empire · Cusco · Americas

Summary

Pachacuti transformed the kingdom centered on Cusco into the expanding Inca state called Tawantinsuyu.

Why It Matters

Expansion joined contrasting highland and coastal environments under a ruler who reorganized territory, labor, and political relationships from Cusco.

Use It on the Exam

Use Pachacuti to explain how military expansion and environmental diversity shaped the administrative needs of the Inca state.

Key Terms (2)
Tawantinsuyu
The Inca name for their empire, often translated as the Land of the Four Quarters.
vertical economy
Andean access to products from different elevations through communities, colonies, and exchange.
Evidence (2)
  • Pachacuti organized conquered territory into four broad regions connected to the capital at Cusco.
  • Inca expansion linked ecological zones that produced different crops, animals, and raw materials.
Connections (1)

Effect

People (1)
Pachacuti
Inca ruler credited with reorganizing Cusco and beginning the rapid imperial expansion of Tawantinsuyu.

Roads, Quipu, and Imperial Administration

1438–1450

Region

Inca Empire · Cusco · Americas

Summary

Inca roads, runners, storehouses, and quipu records connected distant Andean communities to administrators centered on Cusco.

Why It Matters

Transport and recordkeeping allowed officials to mobilize workers, count resources, move armies, and redistribute supplies without alphabetic writing.

Use It on the Exam

Use roads and quipu to compare how large states solved the shared problems of communication, recordkeeping, and resource mobilization.

Key Terms (2)
quipu
A system of knotted cords used to record numerical and administrative information.
chasqui
A relay runner who carried messages and goods along the Inca road system.
Evidence (2)
  • A wide road network connected provincial centers, state storehouses, and military routes through difficult terrain.
  • Quipu records helped officials track population, tribute obligations, labor, and stored resources.
Connections (1)

Cause

People (1)
quipucamayocs
Specialists who made and interpreted knotted-cord records for administrators.

Mali, Gold, Salt, and Transit Taxation

1235–1450

Region

Timbuktu · Africa

Summary

Mali taxed commerce in gold, salt, and other goods moving between West Africa and trans-Saharan markets.

Why It Matters

Transit revenue funded cavalry and state authority, linking Mali's political strength to control of trade routes and productive regions.

Use It on the Exam

Use Mali to explain how African states converted control of trade routes and commodities into military and political power.

Key Terms (2)
transit tax
A levy placed on goods entering, leaving, or passing through a ruler's territory.
trans-Saharan trade
Caravan exchange connecting West Africa with North Africa across the Sahara.
Evidence (2)
  • Mali controlled access to important West African gold-producing regions and taxed goods moving through its territory.
  • Caravans exchanged West African gold for salt, textiles, horses, and other North African goods.

Effect

People (1)
Sundiata Keita
Founded the Mali Empire and established the dynasty that controlled important West African trade corridors.

Islamic Learning and Griot Memory

1300–1450

Region

Timbuktu · Africa

Summary

Timbuktu combined Islamic schools and manuscript learning with West African traditions of oral historical memory.

Written scholarship and griot performance coexisted, showing that expanding Islam added institutions without erasing local ways of preserving history.

Use Timbuktu to explain cultural continuity and change: Islamic learning expanded while oral specialists retained important social roles.

madrasa
An institution for advanced study in Islamic subjects and related fields of learning.
griot
A West African oral historian and performer who preserves genealogies and accounts of rulers.
Evidence (2)
  • Timbuktu developed a reputation for Islamic scholarship, schools, and manuscript culture.
  • Griots continued to preserve dynastic and community memory through recitation and music.

Cause

Related Event

griots
Specialists who preserved genealogies, political memory, and community histories through oral performance.

Mansa Musa's Pilgrimage

1324

Region

Timbuktu · Africa

Summary

Mansa Musa traveled to Mecca, displayed Mali's wealth, and returned with stronger ties to Islamic learning.

Why It Matters

The pilgrimage advertised Mali's resources abroad and helped its ruler use Islamic patronage to reinforce authority and scholarly life at home.

Use It on the Exam

Use the pilgrimage to explain how an African ruler employed religion and wealth to build legitimacy and strengthen interregional connections.

Key Terms (2)
hajj
The pilgrimage to Mecca required of Muslims who are able to undertake it.
patronage
Political and financial support given to religious institutions, scholars, artists, or builders.

Atlantic Constraints and Overseas Expansion

1400s

Region

Maritime Portugal · Lisbon · Europe

Summary

Portugal faced Atlantic opportunities and Iberian limits while Castile and Aragon constrained easy territorial expansion on the peninsula.

Why It Matters

Portugal's Atlantic position, Iberian limits, and primogeniture encouraged overseas routes, but geography created incentives rather than making expansion inevitable.

Use It on the Exam

Use these constraints as contextual causes, while qualifying the claim: political choices, finance, and technology were also necessary.

Key Terms (2)
primogeniture
Inheritance favoring the eldest son, which could push younger nobles to seek advancement elsewhere.
Atlantic position
Portugal's access to Atlantic islands, winds, and coastal routes.
Evidence (2)
  • Castile and Aragon occupied much of the neighboring Iberian land frontier available to Portuguese expansion.
  • Portuguese sailors used Atlantic islands and the African coast as stages for increasingly ambitious voyages.
Connections (1)

Effect

People (1)
Portuguese nobles and merchants
Backed voyages offering traders, the crown, and younger noble sons new paths to wealth and status.

Navigation Knowledge and State Sponsorship

1400s

Region

Maritime Portugal · Lisbon · Europe

Summary

Portuguese voyages combined compass and astrolabe use with lateen and square sails, shipbuilding experience, and royal finance.

Why It Matters

Knowledge from multiple Afro-Eurasian traditions became more powerful when the Portuguese state financed voyages and sustained repeated experimentation.

Use It on the Exam

Link borrowed navigational knowledge to state capacity; neither technology alone nor royal ambition alone explains sustained exploration.

Key Terms (2)
astrolabe
An instrument sailors adapted to estimate latitude by observing celestial bodies.
caravel rig
A later mixed Portuguese sail plan combining triangular lateen sails with square sails.
Evidence (2)
  • Portuguese navigators used the compass and astrolabe alongside accumulated Mediterranean, African, and Asian knowledge.
  • Royal sponsorship paid for ships, crews, information gathering, and repeated voyages along the African coast.
Connections (2)

Cause

Effect

People (1)
Prince Henry the Navigator
Sponsored Portuguese exploration and concentrated navigators, mapmakers, and royal resources on Atlantic and African routes.

1488–1498

Region

Maritime Portugal · Lisbon · Europe

Summary

Bartolomeu Dias rounded southern Africa in 1488, and Vasco da Gama reached India by sea in 1498.

Why It Matters

The route around the Cape of Good Hope connected Portugal directly to Indian Ocean commerce and redirected some exchange through Atlantic-facing ports.

The southern African cape whose rounding opened a sea route toward the Indian Ocean.
sea route to India
The oceanic passage around Africa that let Portuguese ships reach Indian Ocean ports.
Evidence (2)
  • Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488 and demonstrated that the Atlantic connected to waters leading east.

Cause

Indian Ocean Trade before Portuguese Arrival

1450–1500

Region

Portuguese Trading-Post Empire · Malacca · Asia

Summary

Muslim, Hindu, and Southeast Asian merchants used monsoon winds to exchange goods through Malacca long before Portuguese conquest.

Why It Matters

Portuguese sailors entered a mature commercial system they did not create, changing control at strategic ports without originating Indian Ocean trade.

Use Malacca for CCOT: Portuguese coercion changed parts of the network while Asian merchants, monsoons, and older routes continued.

monsoon winds
Seasonally reversing winds that structured Indian Ocean sailing schedules.
entrepot
A port where merchants store, exchange, and re-export goods from several regions.
Evidence (2)
  • Merchants timed voyages to predictable monsoon cycles before any Portuguese ship reached Malacca.
  • Malacca already linked textiles, spices, ceramics, and other goods moving among Asian markets.

Effect

Related Event

Muslim, Hindu, and Southeast Asian merchants
Sustained commercial communities and seasonal voyages linking Malacca to wider maritime networks.

After conquering Malacca in 1511, Portuguese forces used forts, cannon, and cartaz passes to tax and redirect maritime traffic.

Afonso de Albuquerque's strategy built a trading-post empire controlling selected sea lanes and ports rather than most inland territory.

Asian Responses and the Limits of Portuguese Power

1500–1650

Region

Portuguese Trading-Post Empire · Malacca · Asia

Summary

Asian states and merchants resisted, negotiated with, or redirected trade around Portuguese pressure in ways that varied by place and time.

Aceh and other rivals challenged Portuguese influence, the Dutch VOC later displaced it, and Nagasaki restrictions show that Asian responses were not uniform or passive.

Compare Acehnese, Dutch, and Japanese responses to show how local political capacity limited European trading-post power.

Dutch VOC
A chartered Dutch company combining trade, armed force, and state-backed privileges in Asia.
Nagasaki restriction
Japanese policies confining and regulating selected European trade.

  • Aceh and other powers fought or competed with Portuguese Malacca and supported alternative routes.
  • The Dutch VOC captured Malacca in 1641, while Japanese rulers restricted European access through Nagasaki.

Cause

The Columbian Exchange in the Caribbean

1492–1600

Region

Caribbean Colonization · Santo Domingo · Americas

Summary

Contact joined Caribbean, American, African, and Eurasian ecologies through transfers of crops, animals, people, and pathogens.

Why It Matters

The Columbian Exchange was bidirectional, but unequal power and biological vulnerability made its effects especially destructive for Taíno communities.

Compare transfers in both directions, then explain why bidirectional exchange did not mean equal effects on participating populations.

Columbian Exchange
The transfer of plants, animals, pathogens, and people between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia after 1492.
ecological transfer
The movement of organisms and environmental practices between separated ecosystems.
Evidence (2)
  • Europeans brought horses, cattle, pigs, wheat, and pathogens to Caribbean islands.
  • American crops moved eastward while forced African migration added people and foodways to Atlantic societies.

Effect

Taíno communities
Experienced new animals, crops, diseases, labor demands, and colonial settlement after sustained Atlantic contact.

Disease and Demographic Collapse

1492–1600

Region

Caribbean Colonization · Santo Domingo · Americas

Summary

Smallpox and other Afro-Eurasian diseases caused catastrophic mortality among Indigenous Caribbean peoples who lacked prior exposure.

Why It Matters

Epidemics weakened communities and aided Spanish conquest, but conquest was not automatic because warfare, alliances, labor, and policy also shaped outcomes.

Use It on the Exam

Use disease as a major cause aiding conquest, while rejecting automatic explanations by adding warfare, alliance, and labor evidence.

Key Terms (2)
smallpox
A contagious disease that caused devastating mortality in populations without previous exposure.
demographic collapse
A severe population decline produced by interacting disease, violence, hunger, and exploitation.
Evidence (2)
  • Smallpox and other diseases spread through Caribbean populations after sustained European contact.
  • Mortality combined with warfare, displacement, and forced labor to reduce Indigenous populations sharply.
Connections (3)

Cause

Effect

Indigenous Caribbean communities
Faced repeated epidemics alongside displacement, violence, and colonial labor demands.

Spanish encomenderos claimed rights to Indigenous labor and tribute in Santo Domingo as conquest became colonial administration.

From Tenochtitlan to Mexico City

1521–1600

Region

Colonial New Spain · Tenochtitlan / Mexico City · Americas

Summary

After the 1521 fall of Tenochtitlan, Spaniards destroyed and rebuilt much of the Mexica capital as colonial Mexico City.

Why It Matters

Continuity of place and Indigenous labor accompanied a major change in political power as Spain remade a Mexica center for colonial government.

Use It on the Exam

Use the city for CCOT: rule and landscape changed after 1521, while location and urban importance continued.

Key Terms (2)
Tenochtitlan
The Mexica island capital conquered after siege in 1521.
Mexico City
The Spanish colonial capital built over and through conquered Tenochtitlan.
Evidence (2)
  • Cortés relied on numerous Indigenous allies as well as Spanish soldiers during the 1521 siege.
  • Colonizers dismantled temples and rebuilt institutions while retaining the site as a capital.
Connections (1)

Effect

People (1)
Hernán Cortés, Mexica defenders, and Indigenous allies
Fought over Tenochtitlan in a conflict shaped by Spanish forces and Indigenous enemies of Mexica rule.
Source (1)

Casta and Colonial Governance

1600–1750

Region

Colonial New Spain · Tenochtitlan / Mexico City · Americas

Summary

Colonial institutions distinguished peninsulares, criollos, Indigenous people, Africans, and mixed communities through ranked but negotiable categories.

Why It Matters

Casta labels influenced privilege and office, yet lived identities were more flexible than a perfectly fixed official diagram suggests.

Use It on the Exam

Compare formal hierarchy with lived practice: casta shaped privilege without functioning as a single perfectly fixed racial chart.

Key Terms (3)
peninsulares
Iberian-born residents often preferred for high colonial offices.
criollos
American-born people of Spanish ancestry who could possess wealth but resent peninsular preference.
casta
Flexible colonial labels ranking ancestry and status in Spanish America.
Evidence (2)
  • High royal and church offices often favored peninsulares over wealthy criollos.
  • Casta labels appeared in records, but wealth, family, locality, and legal action could alter status.
Connections (3)

Cause

Effect

Related Event

People (1)
Peninsulares and criollos
Competed for status and office in an order generally favoring people born in Iberia.
Source (1)

Syncretism, Resistance, and Social Change

1521–1750

Region

Colonial New Spain · Tenochtitlan / Mexico City · Americas

Summary

Indigenous and African communities adapted Christianity and colonial institutions while preserving traditions and resisting domination.

Why It Matters

The Virgin of Guadalupe illustrates syncretism, while the Pueblo Revolt comparison shows that adaptation and resistance coexisted rather than simple erasure.

Use It on the Exam

Use Mexico City as a representative anchor, then compare syncretic adaptation with revolt to reject total cultural erasure.

Key Terms (3)
syncretism
Selective blending of beliefs and practices from interacting traditions.
Virgin of Guadalupe
A Mexican Catholic devotion interpreted through Christian and Indigenous meanings.
Pueblo Revolt
The 1680 uprising in New Mexico that expelled Spanish rulers for more than a decade.
Evidence (2)
  • Guadalupe devotion joined Catholic forms with meanings rooted in Indigenous experience.
  • The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 shows organized resistance to colonial labor and religious pressure.
Connections (1)

Cause

People (1)
Indigenous and African communities
Preserved, combined, and defended cultural practices under colonial rule across New Spain.
Source (1)

amsco-apwh-u4 · AMSCO AP World History, Unit 4, Topics 4.6, 4.7, and 4.8

Unit 4 Synthesis CardFrom Imperial Extraction to Revolutionary ChallengeUnit 4 empires generated wealth through silver, plantation commodities, monopoly trade, and coerced labor while organizing colonial societies through legal and ancestry-based hierarchies. These systems strengthened states and merchants, but they also spread rights language, sharpened inequalities, and created groups with reasons to challenge imperial legitimacy. Unit 5 revolutions would contest who possessed sovereignty and rights without immediately eliminating the economic and social structures built before 1750.Exam SkillsCCOTCausation

Which Unit 4 institutions created both the resources for stronger empires and the grievances that later revolutionary movements could mobilize?

  • Colonial extraction strengthened imperial states and commercial elites.
  • Coerced labor and ancestry-based hierarchy produced durable inequality and resistance.
  • Revolutionary rights claims challenged imperial legitimacy more quickly than they dismantled older social structures.

Unit 5 Revolutions

Unit 5 Context CardHow Imperial Hierarchy Produced Revolutionary ClaimsUnit 4 maritime empires accumulated wealth through trade, extraction, and coerced labor while organizing colonial societies through legal status and ancestry. Enlightenment arguments about reason, natural rights, and consent gave people excluded by those hierarchies a language they could reuse against imperial and social authority. Unit 5 follows both the spread of those political claims and the industrial transformation that changed which states could enforce power.Exam SkillsContextualizationCausation

How did Unit 4 institutions create both the grievances and the communication networks that made Unit 5 revolutionary claims possible?

  • Imperial extraction strengthened states while sharpening unequal legal and social positions.
  • Rights language became reusable because it made legitimacy depend on people rather than ancestry.
  • Different groups applied the same language to different forms of exclusion.

Social Contract and Natural Rights

1651–1762

Region

Enlightenment Foundations · London · Europe

Summary

Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu, and Rousseau offered competing accounts of authority, consent, rights, and restraint.

Why It Matters

Their disagreements made social-contract reasoning a flexible challenge to inherited rule.

Compare the thinkers precisely rather than treating their claims as identical.

social contract
An agreement used to explain why people authorize government.

Cause

Hobbes, Locke, Montesquieu, and Rousseau

Former socialist states, newly independent states, and market-reforming communist governments entered a more integrated system of trade, finance, production, communication, and migration under unequal conditions.Exam SkillsCausationCCOT

Which Cold War and decolonization outcomes shaped who benefited from globalization after 1991?

  • The Soviet bloc ended, but borders, alliances, military institutions, and conflict legacies persisted.
  • New states entered global markets with unequal infrastructure, debt, and commodity dependence.
  • Market reform changed socialist economies without producing identical political systems.

Unit 9 Globalization

Unit 9 Context CardFrom the End of the Cold War to a Globalized SystemThe end of the Cold War removed a rival superpower system just as market reforms, trade agreements, container shipping, air travel, and digital communications accelerated the movement of goods, capital, information, and people. Institutions created after World War II gained wider reach, but newly integrated states entered with unequal bargaining power, infrastructure, debt, and access to technology.Exam SkillsContextualizationCausation

How did the end of the Cold War and falling transportation and information costs change the scale and rules of global interaction?

  • The collapse of the Soviet bloc widened participation in a predominantly market-oriented global economy.
  • Technology reduced the cost of connection without distributing the gains or risks equally.
  • Postwar institutions expanded their reach while retaining unequal voting power and limited enforcement.

The WTO expanded a rules-based trade system, and its 1999 Seattle ministerial focused criticism on transparency, labor, and environmental consequences.

Resistance targeted how global trade rules were made and whose interests they served, not simply international exchange.

amsco-apwh-u9 · AMSCO AP World History, Unit 9, Topics 9.6 and 9.9

Unit 9 Synthesis CardFrom Regional Networks to Planetary InterdependenceSince c. 1200, exchange networks repeatedly widened as states, merchants, empires, industries, and institutions reduced the cost of moving goods, labor, capital, and ideas. By the late twentieth century those networks connected production, communication, health, culture, human rights, and the environment at planetary scale, but no world government acquired matching authority to distribute gains, enforce rules, or assign responsibility for shared costs.Exam SkillsCCOTCausation

Across Units 1–9, how did expanding networks change who wrote the rules, captured the gains, and bore the costs of interdependence?

  • Technologies changed the speed and scale of exchange, while political institutions determined access and rules.
  • Expanding networks created recurring inequalities between centers, intermediaries, workers, and environments.
  • Global problems became harder to contain within states even though enforcement still depended on state cooperation.
